outcomes.text: Link particles, atoms, cells and waves as the base for later science.
Use the particle model to explain states of matter, density, gas pressure and changes of state.
Explain melting, boiling, freezing and condensing with the particle model, and tell physical from chemical changes.
Higher tier: explain the limits of the particle model when particles are treated as inelastic spheres.
Define density and explain why it differs between solids, liquids and gases using particle arrangement.
Explain how gas molecule motion links to temperature and pressure at constant volume, qualitatively.
Describe how heating changes a system's stored energy and temperature or causes a change of state.
Explain that mass is conserved in melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing and subliming, and the changes are reversible.
Define specific heat capacity and tell it apart from specific latent heat.
Calculate energy changes when a system is heated, using temperature change and specific heat capacity.
Explain scientific purity versus everyday purity and use melting point data to tell pure substances from mixtures.
Build the nuclear model of the atom, isotopes and electron shells.
Describe how and why the model of the atom changed as new evidence appeared.
Recall the typical size of atoms and small molecules.
Describe the atom as a small positive nucleus with electrons around it and most of the mass in the nucleus.
Recall that nuclei hold protons and neutrons and that elements differ in proton number and can differ in neutron number.
Recall relative charges and approximate relative masses of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Relate differences between isotopes to how their identities, charges and masses are written.
Recall that electrons sit in different energy levels at different distances from the nucleus.
Study cell structure, transport, division and specialisation.
Explain how electron microscopy has improved understanding of sub-cellular structures.
Explain how sub-cellular structures of plant, animal and bacterial cells relate to their functions.

subtopics.title: Transport into and out of cells

outcomes.text: Explain how substances cross membranes by diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Describe mitosis in growth, including the cell cycle.
Explain how meiosis halves the chromosome number to form gametes.
Describe the function of stem cells in embryos and adults.
Explain why cell differentiation is important.
Study wave types, wave measurements and the electromagnetic spectrum.
Describe the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves.
Describe ripples as transverse and sound in air as longitudinal, and how each speed is measured.
Describe evidence that the wave, not the water or air, travels.
Describe waves by amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period, and apply the wave speed equation.
Recall that electromagnetic waves are transverse, share one speed in space and carry energy from source to absorber.
Describe the spectrum groups from radio to gamma, their wavelength and frequency order, and that light is one.
Give practical uses of each region of the spectrum.
Higher tier: recall that radio waves can be made by or induce oscillations in electrical circuits.

subtopics.title: Reflection and refraction of electromagnetic waves

outcomes.text: Higher tier: recall that substances reflect, refract or absorb waves and explain effects through changing wave speed.
Explain how larger organisms move materials around and how the body regulates itself.
Study respiration, exchange, circulation, digestion, nerves and hormones in the body.
Describe cell respiration as an exothermic reaction happening in all living cells.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration, including lactic acid and oxygen debt.
Explain the need for exchange surfaces and a transport system in large organisms using surface area to volume ratio.
Describe the circulatory system and gas exchange system, and how the heart and blood vessels suit their jobs.
Describe substances transported into and out of organisms, such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and dissolved food.
Explain how red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma suit their functions.
Explain the role of sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol in building and breaking down carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
Describe substances moved into and out of organisms, such as dissolved food molecules and urea.
Explain how the nervous system structure, including neurones and receptors, suits its function.
Explain how a reflex arc's structure relates to its function.
Explain how reaction times are measured and recall typical results.
Describe how hormones coordinate and control the body through the endocrine system.
Higher tier: explain the roles of thyroxine and adrenaline and thyroxine as negative feedback.
Study plant transport, photosynthesis and the factors affecting it.
Describe the function of meristems and how they let plants be cloned quickly.
Describe substances plants take in and give out, including carbon dioxide, oxygen, water and mineral ions.
Explain why plants need exchange surfaces and a transport system.
Explain how water and mineral ions enter roots through root hair cells.
Explain how xylem suits its function.
Describe transpiration including stomata structure and function.
Explain how light, air movement and temperature affect plant water uptake.
Recall that chromatography uses a stationary and a mobile phase and separation depends on distribution between them.
Interpret chromatograms, including measuring Rf values.
Suggest chromatography methods to tell pure from impure substances.
Describe photosynthesis as an endothermic reaction and what the plant does with the glucose.

subtopics.title: Factors affecting the rate of photosynthesis

outcomes.text: Explain how temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affect the rate of photosynthesis.
Higher tier: explain how these factors interact to limit the rate.
Describe translocation and explain how phloem suits its function.
Explain how communicable diseases spread in plants.
Explain how plant disease spread can be reduced or prevented, with at least one example.
Link lifestyle, radiation and disease to the balance within the body.
Study how lifestyle, hormones and treatments affect health.
Describe the relationship between health and disease.
Describe types of disease, including communicable and non-communicable.
Recall that many non-communicable diseases come from several interacting factors.
Explain how exercise, diet, alcohol and smoking affect disease rates locally, nationally and globally.
Evaluate treatments for cardiovascular disease such as statins, stents, valve replacement and transplants.
Explain why a constant internal environment must be kept despite internal and external change.
Explain how insulin controls blood sugar.
Higher tier: explain how glucagon works with insulin.
Compare Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes and how each is treated.
Describe the roles of hormones in human reproduction, including the menstrual cycle.
Higher tier: explain how FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone interact in the cycle.
Explain the use of hormones in contraception and evaluate hormonal and non-hormonal methods.
Higher tier: explain the use of hormones in treating infertility, including IVF.
Study ionising radiation, radioactive decay and the hazards.
Recall that electron arrangements change when atoms absorb or emit electromagnetic radiation.
Recall that unstable nuclei emit alpha, beta, neutrons or gamma and how nuclear mass and charge change.
Use names and symbols of nuclei and particles to write balanced decay equations.
Explain half-life and how it relates to the random nature of decay.
Recall how well alpha, beta and gamma radiation penetrate materials.
Recall the difference between contamination and irradiation and compare their hazards.
Recall that atomic and nuclear changes can produce and absorb radiation over a wide frequency range.
Describe the hazardous effects of ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays on body tissue.
Recall that atoms become ions by losing outer electrons.
Describe cancer as changes in cells leading to uncontrolled growth and division.
Study how disease spreads, the body's defences, and medicines.
Explain how communicable diseases from viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi spread in animals.
Describe at least one common human infection and sexually transmitted infections, including HIV/AIDS.
Explain how the spread of these diseases can be reduced or prevented.
Describe the non-specific defences of the human body against pathogens.
Explain the role of the immune system in defending against disease.
Explain how vaccines prevent and treat disease.
Explain how medicines such as antibiotics and painkillers prevent and treat disease.
Explain that many useful materials, such as medicines, are formulations of mixtures.
Describe how new medicines are discovered and developed, including preclinical and clinical testing.
Explain benefits and risks, practical and ethical, of using gene technology in medicine.
Discuss potential benefits and risks of using stem cells in medicine.

subtopics.title: Interactions between different types of disease

outcomes.text: Describe how different types of disease can interact.
Explain how living and non-living systems change over time, from atmosphere to genes.
Study the atmosphere's history, cycles, climate change and water supply.
Describe how an oxygen-rich atmosphere is thought to have developed over time.
Recall how materials cycle through the living and non-living parts of an ecosystem.
Explain the importance of the carbon cycle to living organisms.
Describe photosynthetic organisms as the main producers of food and biomass.
Explain the role of microorganisms in cycling materials in an ecosystem.
Describe the greenhouse effect as radiation interacting with matter.
Higher tier: recall that substances absorb, transmit or reflect waves depending on wavelength.
Evaluate evidence for human causes of climate change, including the carbon dioxide and fossil fuel link, and the uncertainties.
Describe potential effects of more carbon dioxide and methane on climate and how they can be mitigated.
Describe sources of carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates, and the problems they cause.
Explain the importance of the water cycle to living organisms.
Describe the main methods of making potable water available, including treating waste, ground and salt water.
Describe, explain and give examples of simple distillation.
Study ecosystems, populations, biodiversity and human impact.

subtopics.title: Levels of organisation in an ecosystem

outcomes.text: Describe the levels of organisation in an ecosystem from individual organisms to the whole ecosystem.
Describe the importance of interdependence and competition in a community.
Explain how some abiotic and biotic factors affect communities.
Describe how to run a field investigation into distribution and abundance of organisms and find numbers in an area.
Explain benefits and challenges of keeping local and global biodiversity.
Describe negative human interactions with ecosystems and explain their impact on biodiversity.
Describe positive human interactions with ecosystems and explain their impact on biodiversity.
Study genes, chromosomes and how characteristics are inherited.
Explain the terms gamete, chromosome and gene.
Describe DNA as a polymer of two strands forming a double helix.
Describe the genome as the entire genetic material of an organism.
Describe how sex is determined in humans.
Explain single gene inheritance.
Predict the results of single gene crosses.
Explain allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous and heterozygous.
Describe simply how the genome and environment shape an organism's phenotype.
Explain genotype and phenotype.
Recall that most features come from many genes rather than a single gene.
Study mutation, natural selection, classification and breeding.
State that there is usually plenty of genetic variation within a species.
Recall that variants arise from mutations and most have no effect on the phenotype.
Describe evolution as change in inherited characteristics through natural selection, which can form new species.
Explain how natural selection favours variants best suited to their environment.
Describe evidence for evolution, including fossils and antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

subtopics.title: Identification and classification of living things

outcomes.text: Describe how developments in biology have changed classification systems.
Explain the impact of selective breeding of food plants and domesticated animals.
Describe genetic engineering as modifying an organism's genome to add desirable characteristics.
Higher tier: describe the main steps in genetic engineering.
Explain benefits and risks, practical and ethical, of gene technology in modern agriculture.
Use the periodic table and chemical quantities as a shared language of chemistry.
Link the periodic table to atomic structure and study groups 0, 1 and 7.

subtopics.title: Atomic number and the periodic table

outcomes.text: Explain how an element's position in the periodic table relates to its electron arrangement and atomic number.
Explain in terms of isotopes how this changes Mendeleev's arrangement.
Explain how atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their place in the periodic table.
Explain how elements' reactions relate to electron arrangement and atomic number.
Recall the simple properties of Group 0.
Explain how Group 0 properties depend on outer shell electrons and predict trends down the group.
Recall the simple properties of Group 1.
Explain how Group 1 properties depend on outer shell electrons and predict trends down the group.
Recall the simple properties of Group 7.
Explain how Group 7 properties depend on outer shell electrons and predict trends down the group.
Use quantitative methods for formulae, equations and reacting amounts.
Use names and symbols of common elements and compounds and conservation of mass to write balanced chemical equations.
Higher tier: write half equations.
Use chemical symbols to write formulae of elements and simple covalent and ionic compounds.
Describe physical states of reactants and products using state symbols.
Recall and use the law of conservation of mass.
Explain observed changes in mass in non-enclosed systems using the particle model.
Calculate relative formula masses of species separately and in a balanced equation.
Calculate percentage by mass in a compound from relative formula mass and atomic masses.
Higher tier: relate the mass of a substance to its amount in moles and back.
Higher tier: recall and use the definitions of the Avogadro constant and the mole.
Higher tier: deduce an equation's balancing numbers from masses and explain the effect of a limiting reactant.
Higher tier: use a balanced equation to calculate reactant or product masses.
Higher tier: relate the mass of solute and volume of solution to concentration.

units.title: 4.6 Interactions over small and large distances

outcomes.text: Study forces and bonds between atoms, molecules and larger structures.
Study forces as vectors, work, weight and energy stores.
Recall how objects interact by gravity, electrostatics, magnetism and contact, and show these forces as vectors.
Higher tier: describe forces on an object with free body diagrams, including resultant and balanced forces.
Describe and calculate energy changes when forces do work on a system.
Use work done, force and distance moved, describing the energy transfer.
Define weight, how it is measured, and its relation to gravitational field strength.
Calculate the energy of an object raised above ground level.
Explain with examples that stretching, bending or compressing needs more than one force.
Describe elastic versus inelastic distortion and force-extension for a spring, including linear and non-linear cases.
Calculate a spring constant in linear cases.

subtopics.title: Energy stored in a stretched spring

outcomes.text: Calculate the energy associated with a stretched spring.
Explain properties of materials through their bonding and structure.
Describe and compare bonds in ionic compounds, simple molecules, giant covalent structures, polymers and metals.
Explain chemical bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and electron transfer.
Construct dot and cross diagrams for simple ionic substances.
Deduce an empirical formula from atom numbers or a model, and the reverse.
Use formulae of common ions to deduce compound formulae.
Explain how properties of ionic materials relate to bond types, strengths and arrangement.
Explain chemical bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and sharing electrons.
Construct dot and cross diagrams for simple covalent substances.
Deduce an empirical formula from atom numbers or a model, and the reverse.

subtopics.title: Properties of substances with covalent bonding

outcomes.text: Explain how properties of covalent materials relate to bond strengths, intermolecular forces and arrangement.
Explain metallic bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and shared electrons.
Explain how properties of metals and alloys relate to bond type, strength and arrangement.
Study magnets, fields and the force on a current.
Describe attraction and repulsion between poles, and the difference between permanent and induced magnets.
Describe a magnet's field, showing how strength and direction change from point to point.
Explain how a compass shows that the Earth's core must be magnetic.

subtopics.title: The magnetic effect of an electric current

outcomes.text: Describe how to show a current creates a magnetic effect and the field directions around a wire.
Recall that field strength depends on current and distance, and explain how solenoids strengthen the effect.
Higher tier: describe the force between a magnet and a current-carrying conductor, using Fleming's left-hand rule.
Higher tier: apply the equation linking force to magnetic flux density, current and conductor length.
Higher tier: explain how the motor effect force makes electric motors rotate.
Study motion, forces, electricity and chemical reactions that matter for safe travel and daily life.
Study speed, acceleration, Newton's laws, momentum, energy and road safety.
Explain the vector-scalar distinction for displacement, distance, velocity and speed.
Recall typical speeds for wind, sound, walking, running, cycling and transport.
Measure distances and times, calculate speeds, and use graphs to find speeds and accelerations.
Higher tier: explain with examples that circular orbit means constant speed but changing velocity.
Recall the acceleration in free fall and estimate everyday accelerations.
Apply Newton's First Law to objects moving at uniform velocity and objects whose speed or direction changes.
Apply Newton's Second Law in calculations linking force, mass and acceleration.
Higher tier: explain that inertial mass measures how hard it is to change velocity, defined as force over acceleration.
Recall Newton's Third Law and apply it to equilibrium examples.
Higher tier: define momentum and describe examples in collisions.
Calculate the energy of a moving body.
Describe energy store changes for a moving object hitting an obstacle or being accelerated by a constant force.
Explain the factors affecting vehicle stopping distance in emergencies and the safety implications.
Explain the dangers of large decelerations and describe energy changes when a vehicle slows.
Study circuits, mains electricity, power and the National Grid.
Recall that current is the rate of charge flow, needing a potential difference and a closed circuit.
Recall and use the relationship between charge, current and time.
Recall how current depends on resistance and potential difference and apply V = IR for ohmic resistors.
Explain how resistance changes in lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs and how circuits explore this.
Describe series and parallel circuits and why resistance rises in series and falls in parallel.
Calculate currents, potential differences and resistances in dc series circuits and explain their use.
Draw dc series circuits with standard symbols, including diodes, LDRs and thermistors.
Recall that UK mains is ac at 50 Hz and about 230 volts, and explain how dc differs from ac.
Recall the functions of live, neutral and earth wires and their potential differences.
Explain why a live wire is dangerous even with the switch open, and the danger of connecting live to earth.
Explain with examples that power is the rate of energy transfer.
Explain how power in a circuit device relates to potential difference, current and energy changes.
Describe how energy moves from batteries and mains to motors or heaters in domestic devices.
Describe the changes in stored energy when a device is used, such as an electric kettle.
Describe with examples how appliance power ratings relate to energy changes in use.
Describe and calculate energy changes when a current does work.
Recall that grid power moves at high voltage and is lowered locally, and explain why this is efficient.
Study acid reactions, salts, energy changes and pH.
Recall that acids react with some metals and with carbonates, and write equations predicting products.
Describe tests to identify gases such as hydrogen and carbon dioxide.
Higher tier: explain that metal-acid reactions are redox reactions, and identify what is oxidised and reduced.
Describe neutralisation as acid reacting with alkali to form a salt plus water.
Describe, explain and give examples of filtration and crystallisation.
Suggest suitable purification techniques from information about the substances.
Tell endothermic from exothermic reactions using temperature change of the surroundings.
Recall that acids form hydrogen ions in water and alkali solutions contain hydroxide ions.
Higher tier: use common ion formulae to write balanced ionic equations.
Recall that acidity and alkalinity are measured by pH.
Recognise that neutralisation is hydrogen ions reacting with hydroxide ions to form water.
Higher tier: use and explain dilute, concentrated, weak and strong in relation to acids.
Higher tier: recall that each tenfold rise in hydrogen ion concentration lowers pH by one.
Higher tier: describe neutrality and relative acidity in terms of hydrogen ion concentration and pH.

topics.title: 4.7.4 The rate and extent of chemical change

outcomes.text: Study reaction rates, catalysts, enzymes and equilibrium.
Describe the effect of temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area on reaction rate.
Suggest practical methods for finding the rate of a given reaction.

subtopics.title: The effect of surface area on rates of reaction

outcomes.text: Explain how smaller pieces of a solid affect reaction rate in terms of surface area to volume ratio.

subtopics.title: The effect of temperature, concentration and pressure on rates of reaction

outcomes.text: Explain how changes in temperature, concentration and pressure affect rate through frequency and energy of collisions.
Explain activation energy as the energy needed for a reaction to occur.
Draw and label reaction profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions, marking activation energy.
Higher tier: calculate reaction energy changes from bond making and bond breaking energies.
Describe the characteristics of catalysts and their effect on rates of reaction.
Identify catalysts in reactions.
Explain catalytic action in terms of activation energy.
Recall that enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
Explain how enzymes work, including the active site, specificity and factors affecting the rate.
Recall that some reactions can be reversed by changing conditions.
Recall that dynamic equilibrium happens when forward and reverse rates are equal.

subtopics.title: Factors affecting the position of equilibrium

outcomes.text: Higher tier: predict the effect of changing reaction conditions on equilibrium position.
Higher tier: predict the effect of changing concentration and suggest conditions for a product.
Higher tier: predict the effect of changing temperature on equilibrium position.
Higher tier: predict the effect of changing pressure on equilibrium position.

topics.title: 4.7.5 Atoms into ions and ions into atoms

outcomes.text: Study reactivity, electrolysis and electron transfer.
Explain how metal reactions with water or dilute acids relate to the tendency to form positive ions.
Describe electrolysis in terms of the ions present and reactions at electrodes.
Recall that metals or hydrogen form at the cathode and non-metals at the anode when using inert electrodes.
Describe competing reactions when aqueous solutions of ionic compounds are electrolysed, in terms of the species present.
Describe tests to identify gases including oxygen, hydrogen and chlorine.
Higher tier: explain reduction and oxidation as electron gain or loss and identify species oxidised and reduced.

units.title: 4.8 Guiding Spaceship Earth towards a sustainable future

outcomes.text: Use carbon chemistry, resources and energy ideas to work toward sustainability.
Study forms of carbon, hydrocarbons and how crude oil is processed.

subtopics.title: Bonding and structure in forms of carbon

outcomes.text: Explain properties of diamond, graphite, fullerenes and graphene using their structures and bonding.
Recall that crude oil is a main source of hydrocarbons and feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
Recognise that crude oil is a finite resource.
Recall that carbon can form four covalent bonds.
Explain that carbon's ability to form chains and rings gives a vast array of organic compounds.
Describe fractions as mostly alkanes of formula CnH2n+2, the alkane homologous series.
Describe and explain the separation of crude oil by fractional distillation.
Describe, explain and give examples of fractional distillation processes.
Explain how modern life depends on hydrocarbons.
Describe how cracking produces more useful materials.
Study metal extraction, energy resources, efficiency and recycling.

subtopics.title: Metal extraction by reduction of oxides

outcomes.text: Explain reduction and oxidation as loss or gain of oxygen, identifying what is oxidised or reduced.
Explain, using carbon's place in the reactivity series, the principles of industrial metal extraction.
Explain why and how electrolysis extracts some metals from ores.
Higher tier: evaluate biological methods of metal extraction such as bioleaching and phytoextraction.
Describe the main energy resources, compare how they are used, and tell renewable from non-renewable.
Describe with examples where energy is transferred in a system and where a closed system's total energy is unchanged.
Describe with examples how energy is dissipated so it is stored in less useful ways.
Explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfer, such as lubrication and thermal insulation, and effects of wall thickness and conductivity on building cooling.
Calculate energy efficiency for any energy transfer and describe ways to raise it.
Describe the basic principles of a life cycle assessment of a material or product.
Interpret data from a life cycle assessment.
Describe a process where a material or product is recycled for a different use and explain why it is viable.
Apply key biology ideas: structure and function, cells, ecosystems, photosynthesis, respiration, cycling, genome and natural selection.
Apply key chemistry ideas: atoms and elements, periodic patterns, bonding, structure, rates of reaction and energy conservation.
Apply key physics ideas: models, cause and effect, fields, differences as drivers of change, proportionality and mathematical laws.
